draft.title: Compound interest
card: With compound interest, the interest earned is added to the balance. The next period's interest is then worked out on the larger amount. So interest earns interest.
The formula is A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ. A is the final amount, P is the amount invested at the start, r is the percentage rate per period (6 means 6%), and n is the number of periods.
Rate and periods must match. For 6% per year compounded monthly, r = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 per month, so the multiplier is 1 + 0.5/100 = 1.005. Then n is the number of months.
Example: $2000 at 5% per year for 3 years. A = 2000 × (1 + 5/100)³ = 2000 × 1.157625 = $2315.25. The interest earned is $315.25.
draft.remember: Multiply by (1 + r/100) once for each period. Match r and n to the same period.

a.q: Priya invests $2000 at 10% per year, compounded yearly, for 2 years. What is the final amount?
a.why: A = 2000 × (1 + 10/100)² = 2000 × 1.21 = $2420. The answer $2400 is simple interest, which does not let the interest earn interest.
a.clue: Is year 2 interest found on $2000 or on the new balance?

b.q: Tom invests $3000 at 12% per year, compounded monthly, for 3 years. Which calculation gives the final amount?
b.why: The rate per month is r = 12 ÷ 12 = 1, and there are 3 × 12 = 36 months. So A = 3000 × (1 + 1/100)³⁶. Using 12% with 3 periods ignores the monthly compounding, so r and n do not match.
b.clue: Convert both the rate and the time to months.

problems.detail: The why says using 12% with 3 periods means 'r and n do not match'. Yet 12% per year with 3 years do match each other, both being yearly. The real error is that neither matches the monthly compounding period. Students who follow the card's rule 'rate and periods must match' could be confused.

check.summary: The facts, worked example and both answers are correct. One small issue: the why for (b) says 12% with 3 periods has r and n not matching, when the real mismatch is with the monthly compounding period.
